explanations.answer: On every one of them alike
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Isaiah lists people and priest alike, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor (Isaiah 24:2). It's a long list and nobody gets skipped. Nobody gets a special lane.

explanations.answer: On the servants more than the masters
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd lean that way, friend. But Isaiah sets servant and master side by side in one list, and the list says "alike." Nothing in the verse says one side takes more than the other. They're named together.

explanations.answer: On the borrowers but not the lenders
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the lenders are on the list too. Isaiah names lender and borrower, then creditor and debtor, both sides each time. The one holding the IOU doesn't get to wave it around and walk free. The whole list is covered.

Not quite, friend. Isaiah doesn't say this is a hunch of his. He says, "For the LORD has spoken this word." (Isaiah 24:3) That's the LORD speaking, not a prophet squinting at the sky and saying "I've got a feeling."
That's right, baker. Isaiah never calls it his own guess. He says, "For the LORD has spoken this word." (Isaiah 24:3) The weight of it rests on who spoke, and the prophet is just passing it along.

You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the everlasting covenant." (Isaiah 24:5) Three things are named there, and the covenant is the third. It's a heavy list, so I'm glad you tracked it.

That's a real treaty from another part of the Bible, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Isaiah names "the laws," "the decrees" and "the everlasting covenant." The Gibeon treaty isn't on his list. You went looking in a different chapter's pantry.

A Nazirite vow is its own thing, friend, and Isaiah doesn't bring it up here. The verse says they overstepped the decrees and "broken the everlasting covenant." That last phrase is the one you want. Keep your ears open for it.
Not this time, friend. Isaiah says the earth's dwellers have been burned, "and only a few survive." (Isaiah 24:6) Only a few, not everyone. I think this one hurts, and it's okay to feel that.
That's right, baker. Isaiah says, "and only a few survive." (Isaiah 24:6) That means not everyone does. This is one of the heavy verses, so we'll take it slow and keep going.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "All the merrymakers now groan." (Isaiah 24:7) The new wine dried up and the vine withered, and the party people go from cheering to groaning. That's quite a change in mood.
I love the energy, friend, but the dancing stops. Isaiah says the merrymakers "now groan," and the very next verse says the tambourines have ceased. Nobody's on the floor anymore.
Sleep sounds peaceful, friend, and that's not what Isaiah describes. He says "All the merrymakers now groan." (Isaiah 24:7) A groan is a long way from a nap.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "strong drink is bitter to those who consume it." (Isaiah 24:9) The singing stops and even the drink tastes different. Like reaching for your favorite cookie and it tastes like the box it came in.
Sweet is the opposite, friend. The verse says strong drink "is bitter to those who consume it." The drink they used to enjoy stops being enjoyable. No sweetness left in it.
I wish it were refreshing, friend. But Isaiah says the people no longer sing and drink wine, and that strong drink "is bitter to those who consume it." Nobody's coming away from that cup refreshed.
That's the word, baker. Isaiah says, "All joy turns to gloom; rejoicing is exiled from the land." (Isaiah 24:11) Rejoicing is pushed right out of the land. Gloom takes its seat.

I'd love some laughter in this part, friend, but it's not here. Isaiah says, "All joy turns to gloom." The streets are crying out for wine, not cracking jokes. I'll save my laughs for a lighter verse.
The dancing has already left the building, friend. The tambourines have ceased and the harp is silent. Isaiah says "All joy turns to gloom," and that's the word that fits the blank.

True, baker. Isaiah says, "The city is left in ruins; its gate is reduced to rubble." (Isaiah 24:12) The gate is the thing that kept the place together, and now it's rubble. Easy one, but a good one to hold onto.
Not this time, friend. Isaiah says, "The city is left in ruins; its gate is reduced to rubble." (Isaiah 24:12) So the statement was true. The gate is rubble, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: A harvested olive tree and leftover grapes
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Isaiah says it will be "like a harvested olive tree, like a gleaning after a grape harvest." (Isaiah 24:13) Both pictures show what's left after the picking is done. I think that's a powerful way to say how little is left.

explanations.answer: A threshing floor and a winepress
explanations.explanation: Those are real harvest-time places, friend, but Isaiah doesn't use them here. He says "like a harvested olive tree, like a gleaning after a grape harvest." Think of what's left on the branch, not the tools.

explanations.answer: A fig tree and a barley field
explanations.explanation: Good harvest thinking, friend, but those two aren't in the verse. Isaiah gives "a harvested olive tree" and "a gleaning after a grape harvest." (Isaiah 24:13) Olives and grapes are the pair.

You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "From the ends of the earth we hear singing: 'Glory to the Righteous One.'" (Isaiah 24:16) After all that ruin, a song rises from the farthest places. Now THAT is a sound worth hearing.

A harvest song would be a classic, friend, but it's not this one. What Isaiah hears from the ends of the earth is "Glory to the Righteous One." (Isaiah 24:16) The song is about Him, not about what they gathered.

That's a confident lyric, friend, but Isaiah doesn't put it in anyone's mouth. The singing from the ends of the earth is "Glory to the Righteous One." (Isaiah 24:16) The glory goes to the Righteous One, not to a city.

That's right, baker. The prophet says, "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." (Isaiah 24:16) The whole earth is singing and he stops with a woe. I'd say he says it twice because he means it.

explanations.answer: With a song of his own
explanations.explanation: I can see him joining in, friend, but the text has him say something else. The prophet says, "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." (Isaiah 24:16) That's a cry, not a chorus.

Relief would be a nice scene, friend, but there's nothing quiet about this line. The prophet says, "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." (Isaiah 24:16) He says it loud and he says it twice.

explanations.answer: No because escaping one leads into the next
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "Whoever flees the sound of panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare." (Isaiah 24:18) It's like closing one pop-up and three more open. Every way out leads to the next one.

explanations.answer: Yes if they run far enough away
explanations.explanation: Running is exactly what the verse describes, friend, and it doesn't end well. "Whoever flees the sound of panic will fall into the pit." (Isaiah 24:18) Isaiah never mentions a distance that makes you safe. The warning is for the "dweller of the earth," wherever they run.

explanations.answer: Yes if they hide up in the hills
explanations.explanation: Hills sound like a decent plan, friend, but Isaiah doesn't offer them. He says "whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare." (Isaiah 24:18) Climbing out of one danger just leads into the next one.
You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "The earth staggers like a drunkard and sways like a shack." (Isaiah 24:20) The ground itself can't stand up straight. That's a picture you won't forget.
I see where you're going, friend, but Isaiah picks a different picture. He says the earth "staggers like a drunkard." (Isaiah 24:20) Same stagger, different comparison.

A tired traveler could stagger too, friend, but that's not who Isaiah names. He says the earth "staggers like a drunkard and sways like a shack." (Isaiah 24:20) The shack comes right after, so stay with him.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "Earth's rebellion weighs it down, and it falls, never to rise again." (Isaiah 24:20) Rebellion is the weight on the earth in this verse. A heavy word for a heavy verse.

Harvest showed up earlier in the chapter, friend, but it's not the weight here. Isaiah says, "Earth's rebellion weighs it down, and it falls, never to rise again." (Isaiah 24:20) Rebellion is the word that fits.
The music already went quiet back in verse 8, friend. What weighs the earth down here is "Earth's rebellion." (Isaiah 24:20) It's the word that belongs in that blank.

That's the first blank, baker. Isaiah says, "In that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below." (Isaiah 24:21) The LORD's reach goes up above, not just down here. Hold onto that.
That's the second blank, baker. The verse says "the kings of the earth below." (Isaiah 24:21) Those kings don't stand above it all. The LORD's reach goes down to them too.
Temple isn't in this verse, friend. Isaiah says, "the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below." (Isaiah 24:21) The blanks want heaven and earth, so skip the temple.
A palace sounds right for kings, friend, and I almost fell for it too. But Isaiah says "the kings of the earth below." (Isaiah 24:21) The blank wants earth, not palace.
A valley is a place, friend, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says the LORD will punish "the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below." (Isaiah 24:21) Heaven and earth fill the blanks.

explanations.answer: The LORD of Hosts will reign
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Isaiah says, "The moon will be confounded and the sun will be ashamed; for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem…" (Isaiah 24:23) The verse gives it right after the "for." That's where the whole message lands.

I like the thought of a brighter sky, friend, but Isaiah doesn't say it. The moon is confounded and the sun is ashamed "for the LORD of Hosts will reign." (Isaiah 24:23) The reason is the reign, not the stars.

That would be a long night, friend, and Isaiah doesn't say it. He says the sun will be ashamed "for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem." (Isaiah 24:23) The text gives the reign as the reason.

Not quite, friend. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, "and before His elders with great glory." (Isaiah 24:23) That's not a quiet backroom, that's in front of His elders with great glory.
That's right, baker. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will reign "before His elders with great glory." (Isaiah 24:23) His elders are there to see it, and the word is glory. Nothing about it is hidden.
